Commentary Outlines Learning Health Systems Framework for Responsible Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Implementation

A commentary published in Health Research Policy and Systems reports that the translation of artificial intelligence into routine healthcare remains inconsistent and uneven, as demonstrated by national hospital survey data showing that fewer than half of 3,560 surveyed United States hospitals have adopted artificial intelligence predictive models. The authors observe that adoption has clustered geographically, with significantly lower uptake reported in hospitals serving higher-need communities. Furthermore, among the facilities that have introduced these predictive tools, nearly half reported that they do not evaluate model accuracy, more than half do not evaluate algorithmic bias, and few maintain systematic monitoring processes once models enter active clinical workflows.

The authors explain that these empirical patterns reflect a fundamental implementation challenge rather than a purely technical limitation. While artificial intelligence tools frequently demonstrate strong technical performance in controlled research environments, their real-world clinical performance is dynamic rather than static. Unlike many conventional healthcare innovations, algorithmic performance shifts over time alongside changing clinical workflows, variations in underlying data pipelines, and demographic drift across patient populations. Consequently, the authors argue that artificial intelligence tools cannot be treated as isolated technological interventions that are simply deployed, but instead require mechanisms for continuous, ongoing evaluation and adaptation.

Implementation science offers established conceptual tools to evaluate these organizational conditions, particularly through determinant frameworks and implementation process frameworks. The commentary highlights the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research as a determinant framework used to assess barriers and enablers across the inner setting, outer setting, innovation characteristics, individuals, and implementation processes. However, because determinant frameworks are designed to diagnose contextual factors rather than prescribe specific actions, they must be paired with process frameworks. In this model, the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change compilation supplies a menu of discrete implementation strategies that can be matched to identified determinants, while the learning cycle provides the structured sequence through which these strategies are enacted and refined.

The authors argue that the Learning Health System framework provides the critical operational bridge that implementation science alone cannot supply. Standard implementation science initiatives typically function as time-limited, linear projects that conclude after reaching predefined endpoints and exhausting project funding. In contrast, a Learning Health System embeds implementation and evaluation activities into permanent operational infrastructure. This architecture incorporates interoperable data platforms, dedicated improvement and analytic personnel, standing clinical governance oversight, and ongoing engagement mechanisms that link patients, clinicians, data scientists, and healthcare managers within routine service delivery.

Within this operational structure, artificial intelligence translation follows a concrete and iterative learning cycle. Before candidate algorithms go live in active care settings, health systems conduct silent evaluations using local institutional data to assess baseline performance. Deployment proceeds in stages evaluated against pre-specified performance and equity thresholds. Once integrated into clinical practice, operational dashboards continuously surveil model calibration, overall accuracy, and subgroup bias across diverse patient groups. When performance shifts are detected, designated clinical governance committees review the surveillance data to authorize scheduled model recalibration or, when appropriate, model retirement.

The commentary integrates this operational cycle with the Monash Learning Health System framework, which emphasizes the deliberate and continuous synthesis of four distinct forms of evidence. Rather than relying exclusively on routine practice data, mature learning systems systematically combine data from routine care with published research and clinical guidelines, implementation science evidence, and stakeholder evidence coproduced by patients, clinicians, and researchers. Structured assessment tools further operationalize this model, including the Translational Evaluation of Healthcare AI framework, which evaluates capability, utility, and adoption, alongside the codesigned Monash Learning Health System Maturity Matrix, which assesses system-level behaviors across eight core domains including prioritization, data infrastructure, and benchmarking.

The commentary reviews existing empirical implementations that illustrate the influence of these organizational conditions. In a prospective, non-randomized multi-site study across five hospitals, the TREWS machine-learning sepsis alert achieved high clinical adoption following multi-year iterative refinements with end users, and prompt alert confirmation within three hours was associated with lower sepsis mortality. Conversely, a qualitative study examining autonomous diabetic retinopathy testing across multiple academic health systems found that long-term program continuation depended on workflow redesign, stakeholder alignment between primary care and ophthalmology, and deliberate site selection. When identical United States Food and Drug Administration-cleared cameras were deployed as time-limited research projects without institutional ownership, the equipment was returned to vendors and the clinical service ended.

The authors emphasize that achieving sustainable clinical integration requires developing specific relational competencies alongside technical capabilities. Because implementation teams and technical developers possess distinct skill sets and rarely collaborate naturally, health systems require deliberate structures that bridge disciplinary boundaries. Relational competencies such as inclusive leadership, transparent communication, and trust building are essential to ensure authentic coproduction between technical teams, healthcare providers, and patients. Academic Health Science Centres, such as the Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation, are highlighted as key entities that assemble these diverse operational groups.

Addressing the emerging divide in artificial intelligence adoption requires concrete system countermeasures targeted at identifiable structural barriers. Lower adoption in high-need institutions is driven by capital infrastructure costs, an analytic workforce concentrated in well-funded academic medical centers, absent or uncertain reimbursement mechanisms, and limited local governance capacity. The authors suggest that health systems can mitigate these disparities by instituting transparent cross-site benchmarking, using maturity assessments to target capability investments, sharing or federating data infrastructure to reduce entry costs, coproducing tools tailored to underserved populations, and routinely monitoring performance across patient subgroups to identify algorithmic disparities.

To manage the operational burden of continuous monitoring without overburdening resource-constrained facilities, the authors recommend embedding artificial intelligence oversight into existing clinical governance and quality-and-safety structures. Each deployed model requires a named clinical lead supported by health system analytics teams and automated surveillance dashboards rather than manual review.
